title: NZ Super Fund, World's Top-Performing Sovereign Wealth Fund, Warns Equity Pullback Looms
excerpt: The Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation, managers of the NZ$93 billion fund with 9.93% average annual returns over two decades, say US-driven equity gains won't repeat — and have cut their own return expectations accordingly.
body:
• NZ Super Fund, ranked the world's best-performing sovereign wealth fund with average annual returns of 9.93% over 20 years, says global equities — led by the United States — are overvalued and will eventually rebalance.
  • The NZ$93 billion fund has cut its long-term equity return assumptions after its five-yearly benchmark review, shifting to "market-aware" assumptions that weigh current valuations more heavily.
  • Co-CIO Brad Dunstan says the fund will lean harder into risk and liquidity management rather than chase the returns of the past two decades.

A top performer turns cautious

New Zealand's sovereign wealth fund — the best-performing such fund in the world over the past two decades — is warning that the equity markets that powered its returns are overvalued and due for a reckoning. The Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation, which manage the NZ$93 billion (about US$50 billion) fund, said this week that prices across asset classes will "rebalance" as the conditions behind two decades of outperformance fade.

The warning carries unusual weight precisely because of who is issuing it. Rankings compiled by international sovereign wealth fund experts GlobalSWF place NZ Super at the top of all sovereign wealth funds over 20 years, with average annual returns of 9.93% after costs and before New Zealand tax — nearly doubling the 6.2% average of its sovereign wealth fund peers and outpacing the 6.8% average of public pension funds. Only Sweden's AP7 public pension fund ranked higher overall. NZ Super also topped sovereign wealth funds over the past five years and finished second over ten.

US equities did the heavy lifting

Brad Dunstan, co-chief investment officer at the Guardians, was explicit about where the returns came from. "A large proportion of our returns over the past 20 years are a result of the continuing outperformance of world equity markets — in particular those in the United States," he said. "One of our key investment beliefs is that prices tend to revert to fair value over time. Of late, we have seen prices across a range of asset classes surge: at some point, those markets will rebalance."

The fund is equity-dominant — its reference portfolio targets 75% global equities, 5% New Zealand equities and 20% fixed income — which supercharged returns during the long bull run in global stocks. The Guardians now believe global equities are overvalued and that higher inflation will compress returns in the near term. "Other things being equal, high prices for assets means lower future returns — especially over a longer term," Dunstan said. "It is hard to see the high absolute numbers of the past few years continuing."

The benchmark itself is being reset

The caution is not just rhetoric. Following the fund's five-yearly review of its benchmark, NZ Super has lowered the expected return of its reference portfolio — driven not by a change in asset mix but by a cut to its equity risk premium assumption. "We did lower [our] equity risk premia assumption by a reasonable amount," Dunstan told Investment Magazine, describing a shift to "market-aware" assumptions that incorporate current valuations rather than a long-term equilibrium price.

That technical adjustment has real fiscal consequences: the New Zealand Treasury funds NZ Super based on a contribution model driven partly by expected returns. "If we lower our forward-looking returns, obviously that means that the government will have to put money into the fund for longer than was previously modelled," Dunstan said.

Impact and analysis

The warning lands in a market already on edge. With the S&P 500 trading near all-time highs and concentration risk flagging — GlobalSWF noted sovereign investors including NZ Super and Norway's fund hold 11% or more of their portfolios in the Magnificent Seven technology stocks — the fund's pivot toward defense is notable. Rather than chase exposure, Dunstan said the Guardians would lean harder into risk and liquidity management, keeping dry powder ready. The fund has long held that it will add risk when markets fall and trim when they rise.

For ordinary retirement savers — including the many Indian diaspora investors whose 401(k)s and retirement accounts are heavily weighted to US equities — the message is a sobering one: the fund that outperformed the world by riding the US bull market now considers that market expensive. Assets that are expensive today have less room to run tomorrow.

What's next

NZ Super will continue its opportunistic active-investment approach, including stakes in local technology and infrastructure. But its posture is unmistakably defensive: hold liquidity, manage risk, and wait for the rebalancing it believes is coming. If the world's best-performing sovereign wealth fund is right, the era of double-digit returns on autopilot is over.
